articles.title: Solar buoyed Europe’s grid amid record-breaking heat and drought this summer
articles.content:
Repeated record-breaking heat waves cooked the European continent this summer, delivering the region’s hottest June on record. A simultaneous, though possibly related, drought shriveled rivers to record lows. In addition to their impact on public health, the dual crises put pressure on Europe’s energy system: Wind power struggled under stagnant conditions created by heat waves, and “thermal” power plants — nuclear, gas, and coal plants — had to reduce their output as European waterways warmed and dried, taking away water used for their cooling systems.

Solar power proved the only major energy source that performed better than normal during Europe’s summer of extremes, experts found. When paired with batteries, it helped supply thousands of AC units during historic hot conditions.

Scientists are still trying to understand why so many recurring heat waves materialized this summer, but studies have found that individual heat events are more likely and more intense because of climate change. The intensity of the June heat wave that scorched Western Europe was roughly 200 times more likely in today’s fossil fuel-warmed climate than it would have been two decades ago, one study found. As the continent continues to warm and Europeans install more cooling systems to cope — just 23 percent of households currently have access to or use air conditioning — experts say this summer provides lessons for the future.

Extreme temperatures in late June bumped up Italy’s power demand by 28 percent compared to the previous week, according to the energy think tank Ember. In France, that number was 14 percent. Electricity and natural gas prices spiked in evening hours as demand grew highest and solar generation ended, with some prices hitting their highest levels since the 2022/2023 winter gas crisis following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

As demand and prices were climbing, power generation in some areas was falling. In the United Kingdom, five gas plants reduced their output by a combined 2.5 gigawatts in generation because heat reduced their cooling systems’ effectiveness. At the same time, heat-induced low wind speeds halved the country’s typical wind farm generation in June.

Historic dryness dropped river levels across Europe: England and Wales reported their driest July on record, while water levels in the Danube River in central and Eastern Europe reached record lows, exposing WWII shipwrecks and prehistoric relics. Europe’s hydropower production hit its lowest July level in a decade, and multiple countries curtailed nuclear power generation as warm, low rivers threatened water supplies for cooling. France lost 18 percent of its nuclear capacity to “environmental factors” in mid-July, Ember found, extending a trend of summertime nuclear outages that has plagued the country in recent years. French nuclear plants often use river water as a vital component of their cooling systems, drawing the water in at natural temperatures and then discharging it back into the rivers slightly warmer. Because French law caps the temperature of this discharged water to protect aquatic life, plants must reduce cooling operations and related power generation when the intake water from rivers is already warm because of heat waves or drought.

But where these sources faltered, solar shone through. European heat waves tend to deliver optimal conditions for solar power: clear, sunny days. Europe’s solar panels produced 17 percent more power during the summer’s heat waves than they normally do, stabilizing the grid as afternoon cooling demand climbed, according to Ember. Battery systems helped deliver this solar power into the evening hours, when heat still lingered and air conditioners cranked to allow households to sleep.

“The next challenge is the evening period. Temperatures often remain high after sunset and AC demand can stay elevated, even as solar production declines,” said Walburga Hemetsberger, CEO of SolarPower Europe, an industry group. “This is why battery storage is becoming such an important part of the energy transition.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

For as much as this summer’s extreme heat strained Europe’s grid, the continent’s cooling demand has a lot of room to grow: About half of households in Italy and Spain have air conditioning, and a quarter in France — compared to 90 percent in the United States.

“There are places where we just can’t do without it now,” Marine Tondelier, national secretary of the Ecologist Party, said this June, a reversal in the party’s longstanding argument against air conditioning because of its greenhouse gas emissions.

France’s state-owned utility plans to spend over $10 billion to adapt its nuclear and hydropower plants to warmer temperatures and lower water availability over the next 15 years, including investments in equipment that cools the water nuclear plants discharge into rivers so that it complies with environmental standards. But adapting to that new demand could also take new generation and storage, especially as grids simultaneously increase demand from data centers.

Solar and batteries have already been growing at a breakneck pace across Europe, with 36 gigawatt-hours installed in 2025, a 48 percent increase over new additions the previous year. Battery installations saw their 12th straight year of growth in 2025, according to industry group SolarPower Europe.

“Extreme price spikes during heatwaves are a blaring signal for regulatory changes that increase power system flexibility,” said Beatrice Petrovich, a senior energy analyst covering Europe at Ember. “Treating this summer as a turning point for energy storage would be an opportunity to remove existing barriers.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on how solar power and battery storage performed exceptionally well during Europe's record-breaking heat and drought, stabilizing the energy grid when other sources faltered. This demonstrates a significant positive impact on energy resilience and climate adaptation for a broad population, with detailed context on the challenges and solutions, highlighting the growing role of renewable energy in climate change mitigation and adaptation.
articles.personality_title: Solar power shines as Europe’s energy lifeline during record heat and drought
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – This summer, Europe faced its hottest June ever, along with a severe drought that dried up rivers. These extreme weather events made it hard for many power plants to run because they need water to cool down. At the same time, wind power dropped due to still air caused by the heat waves.

**What happened** – Despite these challenges, solar power worked better than usual during the heat waves. Solar panels produced 17% more electricity than normal, helping meet the high demand for air conditioning. Batteries stored extra solar energy to supply power even after sunset, when people still needed cooling but the sun wasn’t shining.

**Impact** – This was important because other energy sources, like nuclear and gas plants, had to reduce their output when water levels were too low or too warm for cooling. Solar power helped keep the electricity grid stable when it was most needed. It showed how renewable energy, combined with batteries, can support the grid during extreme heat.

**What's next step** – Europe plans to keep growing solar and battery storage quickly. Countries like France are also investing billions to update nuclear and hydropower plants to handle warmer temperatures and less water. Experts say this summer’s experience highlights the need for more flexible energy systems and better storage to handle rising heat and cooling demand.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Solar energy and batteries helped Europe’s electricity grid stay strong during record-breaking heat and drought when other power sources struggled.

articles.personality_title_es: La energía solar sostiene la red eléctrica de Europa durante una ola de calor y sequía récord
articles.personality_presentation_es:

Los expertos dicen que la experiencia de este verano destaca la necesidad de sistemas energéticos más flexibles y mejor almacenamiento para manejar el aumento del calor y la demanda de refrigeración.

articles.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
articles.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered evidence that an enormous ancient cliff system may have helped expose the deepest rocks of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River began carving the landscape seen today.

Led by researchers at the University of Southampton in the UK, the new study suggests that a vast "great escarpment" formed about 800 million years ago as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart.

These towering cliffs may have reached roughly a kilometer in height and extended for thousands of kilometers along western North America. Over time, erosion along this immense rocky boundary removed huge amounts of material, eventually exposing ancient crystalline basement rocks that can now be seen in the Grand Canyon in southern Arizona.

A Billion Years Missing From the Grand Canyon

Thomas Gernon, Professor of Earth Science at the University of Southampton and lead author of the study, explained that the Grand Canyon preserves a geological history stretching back about two billion years. Yet more than half of that rock record appears to be absent.

He said: "Our paper suggests the Canyon's basement rocks were progressively brought to the surface as part of an immense escarpment that developed during the breakup of an ancient supercontinent.

"The findings also shed light on the formation of the Great Unconformity, a mysterious gap in the rock record that spans over a billion years."

Published in Geology, the research involved scientists from the University of Southampton, GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences and University of Potsdam, both in Germany, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the USA.

The researchers propose that this ancient escarpment crossed areas that today include Arizona, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri and Illinois.

Prof Gernon said powerful erosion across this enormous region eventually uncovered some of the oldest rocks in North America, with the Grand Canyon providing the best known example.

Reconstructing a Lost North American Landscape

To investigate what the region may have looked like hundreds of millions of years ago, the team combined reconstructions of plate tectonic movements with data showing how landscapes evolve through time.

Their results indicate that when Rodinia was fragmenting, the future Grand Canyon sat in roughly the same position relative to the continental edge as major escarpments found today in places such as South Africa and Brazil.

Over tens of millions of years, the giant cliff system would have gradually migrated inland as erosion wore it down. The researchers estimate that this process could have removed as much as eight kilometers of rock in some locations.

That prediction agrees with other geological evidence showing that roughly five to ten kilometers of rock disappeared from parts of the region long before the modern Grand Canyon formed.

"This long-lived tectonic landscape provides a missing piece in understanding why erosion associated with the Great Unconformity varies so dramatically across the southwestern US," said Prof Gernon.

He added: "Our work suggests that tectonic uplift related to continental rifting and breakup created both steep slopes and high ground, providing the mountainous terrain that rivers and glaciers could readily erode."

An Ancient Mountain Rim That Reshaped North America

The influence of this enormous escarpment may have extended far beyond the area that eventually became the Grand Canyon.

By producing a long-lived mountainous rim around western Laurentia -- the ancient core of North America -- the landscape may have shaped the paths of rivers, determined where sediments collected, and influenced when rising seas spread across the continent before the so-called Cambrian explosion, a period when complex life diversified rapidly.

Prof Gernon added: "Today's escarpments in Africa, Brazil, India and Antarctica provide windows into the forces that shape continents over hundreds of millions of years.

"By comparing Grand Canyon's ancient history with active landscapes like the Great Escarpment of South Africa, we're able to see North America's most iconic geologic landmark in an entirely new light.

"Our findings could help geologists reinterpret other ancient continental interiors where similarly large gaps occur in records, offering a better understanding of how Earth's continents have changed over hundreds of millions of years."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about the ancient geological history of the Grand Canyon, revealing how a massive cliff system formed nearly a billion years ago shaped the landscape and explains missing geological records. This breakthrough enhances understanding of continental evolution and Earth's history, with broad implications for geology and environmental science.
articles.personality_title: Ancient cliff system reveals lost billion-year history of the Grand Canyon
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Grand Canyon is famous for its deep, colorful layers of rock that tell Earth's story. However, scientists have long noticed that a huge chunk of this story, spanning about a billion years, seems to be missing from the canyon’s rock layers.

**What happened** – Researchers from several universities found evidence that a giant cliff, nearly a kilometer high and stretching thousands of kilometers, formed about 800 million years ago. This cliff appeared when the supercontinent Rodinia began to break apart. Over millions of years, erosion wore down these cliffs, uncovering the oldest rocks now visible in the Grand Canyon.

**Impact** – This discovery helps explain why so much of North America’s ancient geological record is missing. It shows that the Grand Canyon’s oldest rocks were exposed long before the Colorado River carved the canyon we see today. Understanding this ancient cliff system gives scientists a clearer picture of how the continent’s landscape changed over hundreds of millions of years.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will use this new knowledge to study other places with missing rock records and compare the Grand Canyon’s history to similar cliffs around the world. This could lead to better ideas about how Earth’s continents formed and changed over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A lost giant cliff from nearly a billion years ago helped shape the Grand Canyon’s oldest rocks and explains why much of North America’s early geological history is missing.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un ancien système de falaises révèle un milliard d’années d’histoire oubliée du Grand Canyon
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Grand Canyon est célèbre pour ses couches profondes et colorées de roche qui racontent l’histoire de la Terre. Pourtant, les scientifiques ont remarqué qu’une grande partie de cette histoire, couvrant environ un milliard d’années, manque dans les couches rocheuses du canyon.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de plusieurs universités ont découvert qu’une falaise géante, haute d’environ un kilomètre et s’étendant sur des milliers de kilomètres, s’est formée il y a environ 800 millions d’années. Cette falaise est apparue lors de la séparation du supercontinent Rodinia. Au fil de millions d’années, l’érosion a usé ces falaises, mettant au jour les roches les plus anciennes visibles aujourd’hui dans le Grand Canyon.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique pourquoi une grande partie des archives géologiques anciennes de l’Amérique du Nord est manquante. Elle montre que les plus vieilles roches du Grand Canyon ont été exposées bien avant que le fleuve Colorado ne creuse le canyon actuel. Comprendre ce système ancien de falaises donne aux scientifiques une vision plus claire de l’évolution du paysage du continent sur des centaines de millions d’années.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques utiliseront ces nouvelles connaissances pour étudier d’autres régions où le registre rocheux est incomplet et comparer l’histoire du Grand Canyon à celle de falaises similaires dans le monde. Cela pourrait améliorer la compréhension de la formation et de l’évolution des continents.

**Phrase clé** – Une falaise géante disparue, vieille de près d’un milliard d’années, a façonné les roches les plus anciennes du Grand Canyon et explique pourquoi une grande partie de l’histoire géologique ancienne de l’Amérique du Nord est manquante.
articles.personality_title_es: Un antiguo sistema de acantilados revela mil millones de años de historia perdida del Gran Cañón
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Gran Cañón es conocido por sus capas profundas y coloridas de roca que cuentan la historia de la Tierra. Sin embargo, los científicos han notado que falta una gran parte de esta historia, que abarca alrededor de mil millones de años, en las capas rocosas del cañón.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de varias universidades encontraron evidencia de que un enorme acantilado, de casi un kilómetro de altura y que se extendía por miles de kilómetros, se formó hace unos 800 millones de años. Este acantilado apareció cuando el supercontinente Rodinia comenzó a separarse. Con el tiempo, la erosión desgastó estos acantilados, dejando al descubierto las rocas más antiguas que ahora se ven en el Gran Cañón.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento ayuda a explicar por qué falta tanta parte del registro geológico antiguo de América del Norte. Muestra que las rocas más viejas del Gran Cañón fueron expuestas mucho antes de que el río Colorado tallara el cañón que conocemos hoy. Entender este antiguo sistema de acantilados da a los científicos una imagen más clara de cómo cambió el paisaje del continente durante cientos de millones de años.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos usarán este nuevo conocimiento para estudiar otros lugares con registros rocosos faltantes y comparar la historia del Gran Cañón con acantilados similares en el mundo. Esto podría llevar a mejores ideas sobre cómo se formaron y cambiaron los continentes.

**Frase clave** – Un gran acantilado perdido de hace casi mil millones de años ayudó a formar las rocas más antiguas del Gran Cañón y explica por qué falta gran parte de la historia geológica temprana de América del Norte.

articles.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
articles.summary: The Passivhaus standard is growing in popularity as UK homeowners adapt to hotter summer temperatures.
articles.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house, with no air-conditioning is managing to stay remarkably cool.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a practical and scalable adaptation to climate change in housing, showcasing how a 1960s ex-council house meets the Passivhaus standard to stay cool without air conditioning. This represents a meaningful environmental and societal benefit as it addresses the growing risk of overheating in UK homes due to climate change, offering a sustainable solution with broad relevance.
articles.personality_title: How a 1960s house stays cool without air conditioning on hot UK days
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The UK is experiencing hotter summers, with more heatwaves making it hard for people to keep their homes cool. Many houses risk becoming too hot, and experts say this problem will get worse by 2050 if nothing changes.

**What happened** – In south London, a homeowner named Marion Baeli is living in a 1960s ex-council house that stays cool even on days reaching 35°C (95°F). This house does not use air conditioning but meets something called the Passivhaus standard, which helps control temperature inside.

**Impact** – This example shows that older homes can be updated to handle hotter weather without relying on energy-heavy air conditioning. Using the Passivhaus approach means homes stay comfortable while saving energy, which is good for the environment and could help many people across the UK as summers get warmer.

**What's next step** – More homeowners and builders might start using the Passivhaus standard to prepare homes for future heatwaves. This could lead to new rules and support for making houses cooler and more energy-efficient.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A 1960s house in London shows that with smart design, homes can stay cool in heatwaves without air conditioning, offering a sustainable way to adapt to climate change.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment une maison des années 1960 reste fraîche sans climatisation lors des journées chaudes au Royaume-Uni
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Royaume-Uni connaît des étés plus chauds, avec de nombreuses vagues de chaleur rendant difficile le maintien de la fraîcheur dans les maisons. Beaucoup de logements risquent de devenir trop chauds, et les experts prévoient que ce problème s'aggravera d'ici 2050 si rien ne change.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – À Londres sud, une habitante nommée Marion Baeli vit dans une ancienne maison sociale des années 1960 qui reste fraîche même lors de journées à 35°C. Cette maison ne possède pas de climatisation mais répond à une norme appelée Passivhaus, qui aide à contrôler la température intérieure.

**Impact** – Cet exemple montre que les anciennes maisons peuvent être adaptées pour faire face à la chaleur sans utiliser la climatisation gourmande en énergie. La norme Passivhaus permet de garder les maisons confortables tout en économisant de l'énergie, ce qui est bénéfique pour l'environnement et pourrait aider beaucoup de personnes au Royaume-Uni.

**Prochaine étape** – Plus de propriétaires et de constructeurs pourraient adopter la norme Passivhaus pour préparer les maisons aux futures vagues de chaleur. Cela pourrait entraîner de nouvelles règles et aides pour rendre les logements plus frais et économes en énergie.

**Phrase-clé** – Une maison des années 1960 à Londres montre qu'avec une bonne conception, il est possible de rester au frais sans climatisation, offrant une solution durable face au changement climatique.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo una casa de los años 60 se mantiene fresca sin aire acondicionado en días calurosos en el Reino Unido
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Reino Unido está experimentando veranos más calurosos, con olas de calor que dificultan mantener frescas las casas. Muchas viviendas corren el riesgo de sobrecalentarse, y los expertos dicen que este problema empeorará para 2050 si no se toman medidas.

Esta casa no usa aire acondicionado pero cumple con un estándar llamado Passivhaus, que ayuda a controlar la temperatura interior.

**Impacto** – Este ejemplo muestra que las casas antiguas pueden actualizarse para soportar el calor sin depender del aire acondicionado que consume mucha energía. Usar el estándar Passivhaus significa que las casas se mantienen cómodas mientras ahorran energía, lo cual es bueno para el medio ambiente y podría ayudar a muchas personas en el Reino Unido.

**Próximo paso** – Más propietarios y constructores podrían comenzar a usar el estándar Passivhaus para preparar las casas para futuras olas de calor. Esto podría llevar a nuevas reglas y apoyos para hacer que las viviendas sean más frescas y eficientes energéticamente.
